Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(3,1)$ and a general point $P(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-3)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{2x+2}+1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-3)^{2}+(y-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-3)^{2}+{(\sqrt{2x+2}+1-1)}^{2} \\  & =(x-3)^{2}+(\sqrt{2x+2})^{2} \\  & =(x-3)^{2}+2x+2 \\  & ={x}^{2}-6x+9+2x+2 \\  & ={x}^{2}-4x+11.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=2x-4 & =0 \\ 2x & =4 \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=2>0.$ Therefore, $x=2$ is a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=2$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S\,(2)}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S\,(2)} \\  & =\sqrt{(2)^{2}-4(2)+11} \\  & =\sqrt{4-8+11} \\  & =\sqrt{7}.\end{aligned}
$$
